title: Seeing Through Glass: A Rapid Scoping Review of 3D Documentation of Transparent and Reflective Surfaces in Cultural Heritage, from Photogrammetry to Gaussian Splatting
content: Glass showcases, gilding, polished metal, glazes and translucent stone defeat the assumptions of photogrammetry and laser scanning. Learning-based radiance fields such as NeRF and 3D Gaussian Splatting render these materials convincingly, but whether they also measure them reliably is unclear. We conducted a pre-registered rapid scoping review (OSF: 10.17605/OSF.IO/UJRG7) of heritage studies published in 2021–2026. Of 771 records, screened with AI assistance and checked by blind re-screening (κ = 0.81), 51 studies were included. Evidence concentrates on single objects (40 studies); showcases (3) and interiors (8) are rarely addressed. Holes, noise and baked-in highlights recur across techniques, yet most remedies are applied without comparison, and fewer than half of the studies (23) report a metric result for the difficult surface. Under pre-registered evidence labels, no remedy was supported; cross-polarisation, controlled lighting, near-infrared imaging, multi-exposure, sprays, 2D Gaussian Splatting and radiometric correction were emerging for specific surfaces. Radiance fields increased completeness on glass but often reduced geometric accuracy, and 20 of 43 recommended remedies were never tested. We translate the evidence into workflows by case that combine sensors and separate geometry from appearance, and identify controlled metric studies at showcase and room scale as the main research need.
